title: token ignite runbook
content:
Quick notes / scratchbook for the \"Token Ignite\" experiments (short priming bursts to reduce cold-path p99). Personal log — messy, but reproducible steps and raw numbers so I don't forget what worked.

Summary (TL;DR)
- Goal: get p99 cold-path generation latency under 400ms for short requests (<= 128 input tokens, ~64 output tokens) on A100-40 runs by using tiny controlled priming sequences + KV cache seeding.
- Biggest win: a 2-step priming handshake (warm prompt + micro-batch of 3 synthetic short requests) reduced observed cold p99 from ~920ms -> ~360ms in our emulated ingress scenario. p50 improved but less dramatic (+/- 10-15%).
- Cost: priming adds ~0.8k tokens per cold-start client. Need to evaluate across multi-tenant where priming token charge multiplies.

Motivation / Hypothesis
- Many client requests are tiny (prompt 8-64 tokens). Without good priming, the model spends disproportionate time in kernel launch, KV warmup, and small-batch inefficiencies.
- Hypothesis: a short, deterministic priming exchange that (a) warms the GPU execution paths, (b) populates KV cache shapes, and (c) drives the runtime into steady batching behavior will reduce worst-case latencies for the first few real requests.

Environment (repro)
- Cluster: dedicated A100-40GB pool (instance image: redwood-runtime:2025-02-12).
- Model: rw-open-13B-q4f16 (int4 quantized candidate). Runner config: dynamic-batching enabled, max-batch=16, batch-wait-µs=3000, kv-cache=enabled, kv-prefix-cache=on.
- Ingress emulator: poisson arrivals, mean inter-arrival 80ms, 120 concurrent clients (scaled to match typical spike). Each client issues: 1 priming exchange (optional) then 5 real requests spaced 200ms apart.
- Measurement client: local cytoscope runner, instrumented for per-token and end-to-end timing; collects p50/p90/p95/p99, QPS, and GPU util.

Commands (how I ran it)
- Simple generation (no priming):
  curl -s -X POST \
    -H \"Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_KEY\" \
    -H \"Content-Type: application/json\" \
    https://api.redwood.dev/v1/generate \
    -d '{"model":"rw-open-13B-q4f16","input":"Summarize: The quick brown fox...","max_tokens":64}'

- Priming handshake (two short requests before real):
  # 1) warm prompt (deterministic, low temp)
  {
    "model":"rw-open-13B-q4f16",
    "input":"[PRIMING] initialize session\nSystem: ok\nUser: ping\nAssistant:",
    "max_tokens":8,
    "temperature":0.0
  }

  # 2) micro-batch of short synthetic queries (3 x ~16-token queries)
  # sent back-to-back to populate batching/KV shapes

Measurement details: each test ran 10k real-request samples across 30-minute windows. Cold-path defined as first real request after a 30s idle for that model-worker (approx matches our idle eviction policy).

Raw results (A100-40, rw-open-13B-q4f16)
- Baseline (no priming):
  - p50: 110ms
  - p90: 260ms
  - p95: 420ms
  - p99: 920ms
  - throughput (sustained): 78 qps (with batching active)
  - GPU util at peak: 43%

- Single short priming prompt (8 tokens) only:
  - p50: 105ms
  - p90: 210ms
  - p95: 360ms
  - p99: 620ms
  - throughput: 75 qps
  - GPU util: 45%

- Two-step priming (warm prompt + micro-batch x3 synthetics) [recommended] :
  - p50: 98ms
  - p90: 190ms
  - p95: 340ms
  - p99: 360ms
  - throughput: 72 qps
  - GPU util: 61% (priming raises util by driving better packing on next requests)

Notes on numbers: p99 improvement is primarily for cold-paths — tail before priming had many >1s events associated with small-batch kernel launches and memory allocation stalls. The two-step priming mitigates those by forcing the runtime into a warm-trajectory and improving subsequent aggregation.

Cross-check on H100 (single-run quick)
- Same model variant compiled for H100 (optimized kernels):
  - Baseline p99: ~520ms
  - Two-step priming p99: ~290ms
  - Absolute latencies lower, but priming still meaningful (reduces p99 by ~45%).

Token accounting / cost implications
- Priming token cost per new client session (two-step): ~820 tokens (8 + 3 * 270 synthetic tokens). If client churn is high (new TCP connections per request), token overhead multiplies.
- For environments with strict per-token billing we need to:
  1) push priming into cheap short model (e.g., 1B distilled) and route subsequent real requests to 13B; or
  2) reuse primed worker across tenants for short TTL if acceptable; or
  3) use a deterministic prefix annotation that is not counted/billed (policy ask).

Observations / interesting micro-behaviors
- Kernel-launch stalls: many of the >700ms events corresponded to a single worker experiencing an accelerator page-fault and a subsequent GPU memory relocation. Priming reduced that frequency by pre-reserving common tensor shapes.
- KV shape churn: multiple tiny requests with variable sequence lengths prevents the runtime from stabilizing. The micro-batch of 3 synthetics (same sequence length, same shape) seems to lock in a common KV layout for a short window.
- Autoscaler interactions: priming increases short-term util and may delay autoscale-down decisions (good for latency but increases cost). Need to coordinate with scaling policies.
- Multi-tenant fairness: in shared pools primed workers can become hot for one tenant and degrade fairness if not carefully isolated.

Quick checklist for implementing token-ignite pattern in production
- Provide a small opt-in flag in client SDK: enable_token_ignite: true/false. Default: false.
- When enabling, SDK performs handshake: 1 deterministic warm prompt (low tokens), 1 micro-batch route (3 synthetics). SDK caches session id -> worker binding for N seconds if possible.
- Add telemetry toggle to tag primed vs unprimed flows for cost attribution (tagging at request headers).
- Consider running priming on a cheaper distilled model and then transparently routing real requests to the heavy model once the heavy model is hot (requires cross-model warm transfer tests).

Next experiments (todo)
- Vary micro-batch size: try 2 vs 3 vs 5 synthetics and measure p99 vs token overhead.
- Try variant with synthetic prompts that mimic expected real-client sequence lengths distribution. Hypothesis: shape-matching is more important than token volume.
- Priming on a cheap 1.3B shim -> switch to 13B: measure transfer speed and whether 13B warms faster if it sees the same key-structure.
- Longitudinal cost modeling: simulate 10k daily ephemeral clients to estimate monthly token delta and extra infra costs.

Open questions / concerns
- Does priming change model outputs distribution for the first real request? We used deterministic low-temp prompts but need to audit for hallucination or bias introduced by the priming content.
- Legal/billing: automatic priming increases billed tokens. UX needs to disclose and possibly provide a cheaper priming model option.
- TTL tuning: how long should a primed worker be held in warm-pool before eviction? (current assumption: 30s; try 60s next)

Raw artifacts location
- Experiment traces + instrumentation are in GH perf artifacts (see linked GH PR).
- Local runner trace directory: /tmp/aria/token-ignite/2025-03-18/ (raw JSON traces, useful for deeper waterfall analysis).

Final quick note
- Two-step token-ignite is promising for reducing the cold-path tail without major throughput regressions. We must balance billing and multi-tenant fairness before enabling globally.

-- Aria

(ps: TODO before handing this to SRE: add automated smoke test that asserts p99 < 400ms on a fresh worker using the two-step priming sequence)
